stories.title: The Man-Eaters of Tsavo
stories.excerpt: In 1898 two lions stopped a railway bridge in its tracks. The story of Tsavo's most famous predators, told by the engineer who hunted them.
stories.body:
In 1898 the railway being laid from Mombasa towards Lake Victoria reached the Tsavo River. A young engineer, John Henry Patterson, arrived to build the bridge across it, with thousands of labourers, many of them brought from India.

Within weeks, work in the camp was shadowed by fear. Two lions were taking men from their tents at night. Campfires and thorn fences were built around the camp, and the lions simply went over or through them. According to the accounts, hundreds of workers fled and the bridge stood unfinished.

How many people died is still argued over. The railway's own records name 28 workers. Patterson's telling puts the toll far higher, and people from the surrounding country may have been killed with no record kept at all.

> “The silence of an African jungle on a dark night needs to be experienced to be realised.”
> — John Henry Patterson, The Man-Eaters of Tsavo (1907)

Patterson shot the first lion on 9 December 1898, and the second after it. With the threat gone the workforce came back, and the bridge was finished on 7 February 1899.

He wrote the story up in a book that made the lions famous across the world. In 1924 he sold the skins and skulls to the Field Museum in Chicago, where the two maneless lions still stand. Hollywood films have followed, including The Ghost and the Darkness in 1996.

You can walk the edge of the story today. Tsavo West has a gate named for the man-eaters, and the railway still runs through the same country.

stories.title: The Green Stone Named for Tsavo
stories.excerpt: Tsavorite, a vivid green garnet, was found in Tanzania in 1967 and followed across the border into Taita Taveta. This is how a Kenyan gemstone got its name.
stories.body:
In 1967 a British geologist and gem prospector, Campbell Bridges, found a deposit of bright green garnet in north-east Tanzania, near a village called Komolo. The stone was beautiful and almost unknown.

Selling it was hard. Accounts differ on why: one says exports from Tanzania were not possible, another that the government took over the mines in 1970. They agree that Bridges followed the same rock belt north. In 1971 he found the green garnet again in Kenya, in the Tsavo country of Taita Taveta, and registered his claims.

He worked there for decades. He and his wife lived on the claim in a tree house, safe from the wildlife around them, and he ran mines near Mwatate, including the one known as Scorpion.

The stone became famous in 1974, when the New York jeweller Tiffany & Co. launched it with a full-page advertisement. It needed a name, and the one chosen honours the Tsavo area where the Kenyan stones came from: tsavorite. Who suggested it is told two ways. Some sources credit Tiffany's Henry Platt, others a gem dealer named Peter Morgan. Both agree on the reason for the name.

Today tsavorite is mined mainly in Kenya and Tanzania. One miner interviewed for the trade press says Kenya produces good stones up to about 30 carats, while larger ones have come from Tanzania. Campbell Bridges was killed in 2009 in an attack near one of his mines, and the gem world mourned the man remembered for discovering tsavorite.

The mines he worked still lie in the hills around Mwatate.

stories.title: When the War Came to Taveta
stories.excerpt: The First World War reached Taita Taveta on 15 August 1914. A border town, a fortified hill and a railway built in a hurry changed the county for good.
stories.body:
Most people think of the First World War as a European story. In East Africa it began within days, and Taita Taveta was one of its first battlefields.

On 15 August 1914 German forces from German East Africa took Taveta, a small town on the border. A police corporal who held his post under fire was the first British casualty of the campaign. The Germans fortified Salaita Hill, east of the town, and from there threatened the Uganda Railway.

The British answered with a railway of their own. A new military line was laid from Voi through Maktau towards Taveta, and by 1915 Maktau was the key British base, holding more than 20,000 troops, about 15,000 porters and great numbers of horses and mules. Voi became a hospital centre.

The decisive fighting came in early 1916. On 12 February the Germans held Salaita Hill against a British Empire attack. On 9 March, after a larger offensive, the British took the hill and reoccupied Taveta.

The fighting involved about 250,000 soldiers across the campaign, and most of them were Africans or Indians. Many of the dead were never named. Today the war graves of Taveta, Maktau and Voi are looked after by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission: 188 burials at Taveta and 137 at Voi.

Local historians are working to have more of these places recognised, from the German fort on Salaita Hill to the railway at Maktau.

stories.title: Mwangeka wa Malowa, Chief of the Hills
stories.excerpt: Born around 1842, Mwangeka wa Malowa led the Taita in resisting outside rule. His name is still remembered across the hills.
stories.body:
Mwangeka wa Malowa was born around 1842 at Mwanda, in the hills of Taita. Accounts remember him as a leader who stood against outside rule in the nineteenth century.

He commanded a Taita force that kept watch over the long trade route running from Mombasa through Taru, Voi, Mwatate and Taveta towards Kilimanjaro. Whoever wanted to pass had to deal with him, and that did not please the coastal traders or the Sultan's side of the trade.

In 1892 a British captain, Nelson, joined forces with the Sultan's allies to break Mwangeka's influence. According to the accounts, it took them about a month just to get into the hills, because the terrain favoured the Taita fighters on the heights. At Mwashoti they met fierce resistance and were driven back.

Mwangeka went to the defence of his people at Mwashoti, even after being warned against it by diviners, and was killed in the fighting. His death was a heavy blow to his people. His second in command, Mnjala wa Ruma, gathered them in the caves of Vuria, the highest peak in the hills, as a last line of defence.

Peace came through mediation, but the trade routes passed into British hands.

The details differ between written and oral accounts, and the people who keep his story are the Taita themselves. His descendants and local historians have worked to record it. Vuria, where the story ends, is also where you will find the highest views in the county.

stories.title: Who Are the Taita?
stories.excerpt: Hill farmers, irrigators and musicians: a short introduction to the Taita, the people of the hills, and the three regions they call home.
stories.body:
The Taita live in and around the Taita Hills and speak Kidawida. The hills hold three main regions: Dawida, Sagala and Kasigau. Taita people from other massifs still call a trip to the heart of the hills "going to Dawida".

Traditionally the Taita lived in clans, each with its own territory in the hills, and leadership followed those territories. Most families have long depended on farming, and the hills' steep slopes are watered by irrigation channels that men built and maintained.

The Taita are also known for their music. The late Fadhili William, a Taita musician, is known for his international hit song Malaika.

There is a quieter side to Taita heritage too. Caves and rock shelters in the hills have long been sacred places linked to ancestors. They are not tourist sights. If you want to learn about them, ask a Taita guide, and respect the answer.

Historians still debate where the Taita came from and how they settled the hills, and the picture seems to be one of many people moving through the Kilimanjaro corridor over a long time.

To meet the hills as the Taita know them, start in Wundanyi, the hill town, and ask someone to show you the terraces.
stories.credits:

stories.title: Mzima Springs: The River That Rises From Rock
stories.excerpt: Rain that fell on the Chyulu Hills years ago comes out clear and cold in Tsavo West, and a glass chamber lets you watch hippos from underneath.
stories.body:
Tsavo is mostly brown. Mzima Springs is the exception, a patch of bright green and glassy water in the middle of the dry country.

The water arrives by an underground route. Rain falling on the Chyulu Hills sinks into the porous volcanic rock, travels below the plains, and comes out clear at Mzima Springs in a series of pools. Some operators also credit meltwater from Kilimanjaro, but the Chyulu Hills are the source most often named.

The springs give tens of millions of gallons a day, and a large part of that is piped to Mombasa. The clear pools you watch from the bank are part of what keeps a big coastal city supplied.

What makes Mzima special for visitors is the view. An underwater observation chamber puts you at eye level with fish, and with hippos and crocodiles moving along the bottom. The surrounding trees draw many birds too.

The pools sit in volcanic country, and the same lava that filters the water has left the black flows and cinder cones nearby.

This is protected park land: follow the rangers' instructions at the water's edge, because the hippos are real and they are not shy.

stories.title: Shetani: Where the Devil Came Out of the Earth
stories.excerpt: A field of black lava, only a few hundred years old, covers part of Tsavo West. Local people named it after the devil.
stories.body:
West of the Chyulu gate in Tsavo West, the ground turns black. This is the Shetani lava flow, a field of volcanic rock that poured out just a few centuries ago, which is yesterday in geological time.

Shetani is the Kiswahili word for devil. The name comes from the belief of the people living nearby that the devil himself had risen out of the earth, and when you stand on the rough, ropy rock it is easy to see why.

The same volcanic activity left caves, and short climbs up cinder cones give wide views across the lava country, the Chyulu Hills and the plains beyond. Birds of prey ride the air above.

The flow is part of the story of Tsavo West's landscape. The volcanic rock is also what filters the water that emerges at Mzima Springs, so the two sights belong together.

Wear sturdy shoes: lava is sharp, and it holds the heat of the day.

stories.title: Islands in the Sky: The Taita Hills' Cloud Forests
stories.excerpt: The Taita Hills rise out of dry plains like islands, and their misty forests hold birds found nowhere else on Earth.
stories.body:
From the plains of Tsavo, the Taita Hills look like islands. They are part of the Eastern Arc Mountains, an ancient chain of isolated ranges, and their forests have been separate from other forests for a very long time.

That separation shapes everything that lives here. The hills are a Key Biodiversity Area, and birdwatchers come from across the world to see two birds in particular, the Taita Thrush and the Taita Apalis, found nowhere else.

But the forests are small and under pressure. Under colonial rule, a great deal of the original forest was replaced by plantations of fast-growing foreign trees. As the population grew, farmers moved higher up the slopes. What remains is a patchwork of precious fragments.

Ngangao, near Wundanyi, is one of them, and its peak reaches about 2,149 metres. Mbololo, another of the hill forests, lies at roughly 1,400 to 1,700 metres.

The forests are cold, wet and quiet, and mist often hangs in the trees.

Walk with a local guide, stay on the paths, and take your litter with you. Here, a careful visitor is part of the protection.

stories.title: A Lodge on Stilts: The Story of Salt Lick
stories.excerpt: Rooms perched above floodlit waterholes made Salt Lick one of the most photographed lodges in Africa. It began as sisal and sheep.
stories.body:
The land under Salt Lick has had several lives. It began as sisal, turned to sheep, and is now the Taita Hills Wildlife Sanctuary, a conservancy that borders Tsavo West National Park.

Two lodges were built there in 1969 and opened to the public in 1973, about seven kilometres apart: Salt Lick and Taita Hills. Both were built to put guests close to the wildlife.

Salt Lick's answer was to lift the rooms on stilts. They stand in circular pairs above the waterholes, joined by suspended walkways, and the waterholes are floodlit at night so nothing is missed. The lodge has 96 rooms in all and an underground tunnel that takes you down to animal level.

It is built around a simple idea: that elephants come to drink, and that the best way to watch them is to be quiet and wait.

Both lodges are now run by Sarova Hotels.

The sanctuary around the lodges is private land beside Tsavo West, and a good place for birds: up to about 300 species have been counted on its walks.

places.name: Tsavo East National Park
places.blurb: The flatter, drier half of Kenya's biggest park, crossed by the Galana River. Most visitors from Voi come in through Manyani Gate.
places.note: The position is the park's centre (2°46′43″S 38°46′18″E), not an entrance.

places.name: Tsavo West National Park
places.blurb: More mountainous and wetter than its eastern twin, with swamps, Lake Jipe, Mzima Springs and a rhino sanctuary, plus volcanic hills and lava flows.

places.name: Mzima Springs
places.blurb: Clear pools that rise from beneath the lava, with an underwater viewing chamber for hippos, fish and crocodiles. Much of its water is piped to Mombasa.
places.note: Position from the NGA GeoNames database.

places.name: Shetani Lava Flow
places.blurb: A field of black lava only a few hundred years old, named for the devil by the people who watched it form. Caves and cinder cones lie nearby.

places.name: Ngulia Rhino Sanctuary
places.blurb: A fenced refuge at the foot of the Ngulia Hills that has helped bring black rhino back in Tsavo.

places.name: Mudanda Rock
places.blurb: A long whale-backed rock, about 1.6 km from end to end, that catches rain and feeds a natural dam where elephants gather. It lies near Manyani Gate.
places.note: Described as about 5 km south of Manyani Gate on Tsavo East's eastern edge; no reliable position found yet.

places.name: Salaita Hill
places.blurb: The German stronghold east of Taveta, and the scene of the 1916 battle that gave the First World War in East Africa its first large fight. Traces of the fortifications remain.
places.note: Also called Iltorrobo by the Maasai. No reliable position found yet.

places.name: Taveta Military Cemetery
places.blurb: The Commonwealth war graves of Taveta: 188 burials from 1914–1918, near the border post. It is kept locked, so arrange a visit through the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.
places.note: On the western side of Taveta town, next to the District Commissioner's office.

places.name: Voi War Cemetery
places.blurb: Voi became a hospital centre for the British in 1916. The cemetery by the police station now holds 137 Commonwealth burials from the First World War.
places.note: The position is Voi town's centre; the cemetery is next to the police station.

places.name: Maktau and its war cemeteries
places.blurb: The key British base of the Taveta campaign, which housed more than 20,000 troops in 1915. A well-kept Indian cemetery has a plinth carrying the names of the soldiers who died.

stays.name: Salt Lick Safari Lodge
stays.description: A lodge of 96 rooms raised on stilts in two levels above floodlit waterholes, joined by suspended walkways, inside the private Taita Hills Wildlife Sanctuary beside Tsavo West. Built in 1969 and opened in 1973.
stays.note: Listed from public information. Not yet confirmed with the lodge: contact them before publishing.

stays.name: Taita Hills Game Lodge
stays.description: The sister lodge of Salt Lick, about seven kilometres away in the same sanctuary. Built in 1969 and opened in 1973, on land that was once a sisal estate and later a sheep farm.
stays.note: Listed from public information. Not yet confirmed with the lodge: contact them before publishing.

stays.name: Voi Wildlife Lodge
stays.region: Tsavo East National Park, near Voi
stays.description: A lodge inside Tsavo East National Park near Voi, used by safari itineraries as a base for exploring the park.
stays.note: Listed from public information, with very little detail. Contact the lodge for facts before publishing.

products.description: Four small coiled sisal coasters in the Taita vidasi style, plant-dyed in earth tones.

products.name: Beaded Keyring
products.description: A small beaded keyring in red, white and blue glass beads, made to order.

products.name: Forest-Edge Honey, 250 g
products.description: Raw honey strained by hand and jarred in the village, from hives along the edge of the Ngangao forest.

products.name: Handmade Leather Belt
products.description: A vegetable-tanned leather belt, cut to your waist size and stitched by hand.

products.name: Tsavorite Silver Pendant
products.description: A small tsavorite in a hand-finished silver setting on a fine chain. Each stone is different.
